record.field: Sixty-three invoices, and the one action on them that cannot be undone.
Sixty-three invoices, and only fifteen of them are your job
August 2026 in Hà Nội: 63 invoices, 25,850,000 ₫ billed. 48 are paid and closed. The 15 that are not are the only rows on this screen that need anything from you.
The list is grouped by service here so the total is readable. In the product it is one row per invoice.

6,150,000 ₫ is outstanding — billed and not yet paid. 1,850,000 ₫ of that is overdue — billed, not paid, and past its terms. The first number is how the business works. The second is the only one you chase.
Reading outstanding as if it were overdue is how an accountant ends up ringing clients who are not late.
Post, Register payment, Credit note, Reset to draft

Post turns a working document into an accounting one. Register payment records money arriving. Credit note issues a second document that reverses the first. Reset to draft undoes the posting — and it is the one worth understanding before you press it.
Posting takes a number that belongs to a sequence

Before posting, an invoice is editable and means nothing outside this screen. Posting assigns it a number from a legal sequence, and that sequence must have no gaps. The document now exists whether or not it was right.

Scope: this invoice, the sequence it drew its number from, and the month's reported totals. Reversible: not by deleting it — a posted invoice is corrected by a second document, a credit note, which is itself part of the record. Check first: the client, the amount and the service description, because those are the three things a credit note exists to fix.
A payment nobody matched is worse than one nobody received

An unmatched payment shows as collected on the Dashboard and leaves the invoice sitting unpaid on the client's record. Nothing looks broken from either side — which is how a client gets chased for money they already sent.
If a client insists they paid, this is the screen to open before you argue.
1,350,000 ₫ is in a nurse's pocket, and that is not your problem

Cash collected on visits sits in transit until it is banked. Operations reconciles it at end of shift — the same figure appears on their Collections screen. Finance receives a balanced number and never chases an individual nurse.
This is one number seen from two departments. Knowing whose job it is saves the phone call.
You posted an invoice this morning and have just noticed the service description is wrong. The filing period is still open. What do you do?
Correct it with a document against the invoice, and check whether a red invoice was issued for it.

Yes. A posted invoice is corrected by a second document, never by editing the first. The red invoice question matters because if one was issued, the correction is also a filing event and not just an accounting one.
Reset it to draft, fix the description, and post it again — the period is open, so nothing is lost.

Let's rethink that. An open period makes this technically possible and does not make it correct: the invoice was already issued to a client, and if a red invoice went with it, the tax document and your books now disagree. The correction belongs on the record, not hidden by re-posting.
Leave it — the amount is right and the description is only wording.

Let's rethink that. The service description is one of the three things a red invoice may be cancelled and reissued for, which tells you the tax authority does not treat it as wording. It is what the client was billed for.
Vietnamese tax invoices — the most consequential screen in the product.
41 of 63, because it is issued on request

A red invoice is a Vietnamese tax document, issued through Viettel V-Invoice. It is not created automatically for every sale — 41 of this month's 63 invoices have one, because those are the clients who asked.
So “this invoice has no red invoice” is usually correct, not a missing step.
Cancel and reissue only when the buyer details, the amount or the service description are wrong, and only inside the current filing period. Once the period closes, the route is a credit note instead.
Anything not on that list of three is not a cancellation reason, however inconvenient the invoice is.
This button talks to the tax authority

Cancelling calls Viettel and voids a document that has already been reported. It is not a local change that you can decide to make and then reconsider — the cancellation is itself an event on your filing record.

Scope: a live Vietnamese tax document, the client who holds a copy of it, and your filing for this period. Reversible: no — the reissued invoice is a new document with a new number, and both the cancellation and the reissue are on the record. Check first: that the reason is buyer details, amount or service description, and that the period is still open. If either is not true, this is the wrong button.
Not everyone who can open the invoice

Cancelling a red invoice is restricted to the tax-compliance group. Being able to read an invoice, post it or take a payment on it does not carry the right to void its tax document — those are deliberately different permissions.
If the button is not there for you, that is the design working, not a fault to report.
A cancellation count that stays low is the healthy state

One cancellation in a month of 41 issued documents is normal. A number that climbs is not a red-invoice problem — it means invoices are being posted before somebody checks the buyer details, and the fix is upstream on the Invoices screen.
A client rings in September about an August red invoice: the company tax code on it is wrong. August is closed. What is the route?
A credit note, because the filing period has closed — cancellation was only available while August was open.

Yes. Wrong buyer details is a valid reason, but the window is what decides the route. Inside the period it is a cancel-and-reissue; once the period is closed the correction has to be a document that sits on top of what was already filed.
Cancel and reissue it — a wrong tax code is one of the three permitted reasons.
Let's rethink that. The reason is valid and the timing is not, and both have to be true. August has been filed; voiding a document inside a closed period reopens something that was already reported.
Ask the client to accept it, since the amount and the service are both correct.

Let's rethink that. The tax code is who the document belongs to — the client cannot use an invoice issued to the wrong entity, so this is not a small discrepancy they can absorb. There is a correct route; it is just not a cancellation.
The triage wall: every open conversation across every channel, most urgent first.

Care Command shows one work item per person, not per message. Zalo, calls, email and web chat for the same family collapse into a single row. Right now this desk has 12 open conversations, 7 needing a reply and 3 nobody has claimed.
The row stores no message text. It points at the Zalo thread and the call log, and builds the timeline when you open it.
You are looking at one area, not the country

Every count on this screen is filtered to your catchment area — here, Hà Nội. For channel traffic the area comes from the channel account the message arrived on: one Zalo Official Account per area. This is why the same wall looks empty to a colleague in Hồ Chí Minh City.

Trần Mỹ Linh messaged the Hà Nội Zalo OA at 07:42 about her mother, Nguyễn Thị Hoa (78). Two unread messages, one missed call at 07:55, and Hoa has a wound-care visit booked for 16:30 today. Score: 110.
Note who is typing. The Zalo account is the daughter's, not the patient's. Hold that thought.

Six terms add up. Needs reply +40, booking within 24 hours +30, unread messages +15, unhandled missed call +10, watch phrase matched +15, ageing +0 — because only 18 minutes have passed. Every operator sees the same 110 for the same facts.
A watch phrase moved this to the top

The phrase “khó thở” (shortness of breath) is on the clinic's watch list. When it appears in an inbound message it adds +15. Watch the line: the phrase in the message travels to the term in the score.
A watch phrase is triage, never a diagnosis. It changes the queue position; it does not tell you what is wrong with the patient.
Claiming makes you the owner. If a colleague claims the same second, exactly one of you wins and the other is told who. Everything after this — replying, booking, escalating — assumes one owner.
Only a CRM Manager can take a claimed conversation off someone else. That is deliberate.

Needs reply → you answer → Waiting → they are dealt with → Closed. Junk? is a branch off to the side, not a step forward. Sending a reply moves the item to Waiting automatically and clears the unread count.
It zeroes the urgency score and drops the row off the wall — and it also marks the linked contact as spam and flags the phone number. Toggle the panel to see the same record before and after.

Scope: the conversation, the contact record, and the phone number. Reversible: the status can be set back, but the number stays flagged until someone clears it, and the next operator sees a pre-judged caller.
On the wall · contact status “New” · number not flagged
Off the wall · contact status “Spam Call” · +84 912 345 678 flagged for every future call
Six doors out of a conversation

Book opens the booking flow with the duplicate check. Log as lead keeps them for later. Escalate pages the {{roleHeadNurse}}, the {{roleOpsManager}} or the {{roleDutyDoctor}} — and needs a lead on the conversation. Reminder, Internal note and Consents leave no trace with the patient.
Internal note and Reminder are the two safe actions when you are not sure. Use them instead of guessing in a reply.
Who is actually on the other end?

The Zalo account belongs to Linh. The patient is Hoa. Whether you may discuss Hoa's wound with Linh is a recorded permission — {{consentPolicyName}} — not a judgement call. Open Consents and look before you answer a clinical question.

Scope: a message you cannot recall, to a person who may not be permitted to receive it. Reversible: no — a sent Zalo message is gone. Check first: the client's Data Sharing consent for this named relation, and whether it is still active.

It is 08:05. Conversation #4172 sits at 110 and asks whether the mother's wound is infected. The Zalo account is the daughter's, and the client's Data Sharing consent for her was withdrawn in June. What do you do?
Claim it, reply that you cannot discuss the details over this account, and escalate to the {{roleDutyDoctor}} while calling the client's own number.

Yes. You answer the person — quickly, because the urgency is real — without disclosing anything you are not permitted to. The clinical question goes to a clinician, and the client's own line is the route that needs no third-party consent.
Reply straight away with what the last visit note said about the wound — she is family and the score is 110, so speed matters most.

Let's rethink that. The 110 is a queue position, not permission. Family relationship is not consent, and a withdrawn consent is an explicit “no”. A sent Zalo message cannot be recalled, and this one would disclose a patient's clinical detail to someone the patient has said no to. Speed is satisfied by replying fast — just not with that content.
Mark it Junk? — the account is not the patient's, so it does not belong on the wall.

Let's rethink that. Junk? is for junk, and this is a real family in distress. Worse, it would also mark the contact as spam and flag that phone number, so the next time this daughter calls she starts pre-judged. Family members messaging on a patient's behalf is normal in home care — it is a consent question, not a spam question.
Connect, prove and watch every channel. The most consequential setup screen in CRM.
Eight channels, one truth about each

This is the catalogue of every channel a clinic can connect: Zalo, Calls, Email, ZNS, WhatsApp, Messenger, Telegram and Web chat. Walk-in is not here — a person coming through the door has no provider and no credentials, so offering a “Connect” button for it could only ever fail.

A connection walks a fixed path: Not connected → Signing in → Choosing what to connect → Setting things up → Testing → Connected. It becomes Connected only when every required readiness check passes. You never type a state in; one server path writes it and audits every move.

{{oaNameNorth}} is a Zalo Official Account in the Connected state, carrying the Hà Nội catchment. Every message that arrives on it becomes a Hà Nội conversation — including Linh's at 07:42 this morning.
One setting decides whose wall it lands on

The area on this account is not a label — it is the routing rule. Follow the line from the account's catchment to the Hà Nội wall count. Change this field and yesterday's conversations do not move, but every new one does.
Point it at the wrong city

Toggle the panel. Re-pointing this one account at TPHCM takes the Hà Nội wall from 12 open conversations to 4, and hands 8 to a desk 1,700 km away that has never met these families. Nothing errors. Nothing warns. The Hà Nội desk simply has a quiet morning.
Hà Nội wall open · HCMC wall open
8 conversations move to a desk 1,700 km away that has never met these families
No error. No warning. Just a quiet morning.
What a green tick does and does not prove

Readiness checks are the reason a connection may call itself Connected: credentials valid, webhook verified, send permission granted, account selected. They prove the connection is capable. Only real inbound traffic proves it works.
After connecting, send yourself one message from a personal account and watch it appear on the wall. That is the only test that counts.

The TPHCM account's grant dies in 6 days. It is deliberately still allowed to send — refusing to reply to patients today would be a worse failure than the warning. That is exactly why this state gets ignored until the morning it becomes Action required and the inbox goes silent.

Scope: every future message on that channel, in both directions. Reversible: yes, by re-authorising — but nothing queues while it is down, so the messages sent during the gap are simply lost to you. Check first: who holds the provider login, before the day you need it.
Action required means a human must go somewhere else

Messenger lost a permission at the provider. Nothing in CareJioX can fix that — someone has to sign in to the platform and grant it again. Until then this channel neither sends nor receives, and the screen says so rather than showing a hopeful green.

A channel shown as connectable is only offered when this deployment actually has an adapter and the tenant has credentials. If nothing is configured yet, the console says nothing is configured — it never draws a Connect button that could only fail.
This is the screen to open first when someone says “we stopped getting enquiries”. Nine times in ten the answer is here, not in the advertising.
A colleague reports that the Hà Nội wall has been unusually quiet since Tuesday, while the TPHCM desk says it is drowning. Both Zalo accounts show Connected. What is the first thing you check?
The catchment area recorded on each Zalo Official Account — including which account is selected on each connection.

Exactly. Both channels being healthy and the volume moving from one wall to another is the signature of a routing change, not an outage. The area on the account is the routing rule, and re-selecting the wrong account during a re-authorisation is the usual cause.
Whether the Hà Nội operators have the right role, since they may simply have lost visibility of the leaves.

Let's rethink that. A role change would hide the whole screen from those users, not move the volume onto a different team's wall. And it would not explain TPHCM receiving more. When work moves rather than disappears, look at routing before permissions.
Re-authorise both accounts to be safe, then see whether the balance corrects itself.

Let's rethink that. Re-authorising takes a connection out of the connected states while it walks the path again — and nothing queues while it is down, so you would add a real outage on both cities to a routing problem in one. Diagnose from the account selection first; re-authorisation is the fix for an expiring or lost grant, not a diagnostic.
Start of shift: what came in, what is waiting, how conversion is going.
Every number here belongs to a period

Nothing on this screen means anything without the selector at the top. Contacts Today is a day figure; Conversion Rate is a month figure. They are never describing the same window, and reading one as if it were the other is the most common mistake this screen produces.
The period also scopes the charts and the feeds below, not just the six cards.
Pending Follow-ups is the early warning

Today it reads 9. That is the count of promises made and not yet kept. It is the earliest visible sign that somebody will be forgotten — long before a complaint arrives, and long before conversion moves.
Compare it with your team's capacity, not with zero. Nine across four people is a normal morning; nine across one person is not.
224 enquiries, and every one is in exactly one bucket

This month: 224 enquiries = 14 spam + 210 real. Those 210 split into 63 booked, 129 leads and 18 lost. Nothing is counted twice and nothing is missing — if the donut and the cards ever disagree, one of them is filtered differently.
Conversion is measured against real enquiries, not all of them
63 ÷ 210 = 30.0%. The denominator is 210 — real enquiries — not 224. Spam is excluded on purpose: counting it would let a bad month look better simply because more junk arrived.
If nobody marks spam, the 14 stays in the real pile and conversion is quietly understated all month. A low Spam Rate is not automatically good news — it can simply mean nobody is marking.
Zalo 96, hotline 58, web chat 34, Facebook 21, walk-in 9, referral 6. They sum to 224. This is the chart that tells you which channel going quiet would actually hurt.
A channel dropping to zero rarely raises an error. This chart is usually the first place it shows.
Every figure opens the records behind it
Cards and chart segments are clickable, and the feeds below are the same records in a list. A surprising number should always be opened, never explained away at the dashboard.
Spam Rate has fallen from 6.3% to 1.1% this month and Conversion Rate has fallen too. What is the most likely explanation?
Nobody has been marking spam, so junk is sitting in the real-enquiry denominator and dragging conversion down.

Yes. Conversion divides by real enquiries, so unmarked junk inflates the denominator and lowers the rate. The two numbers moving down together is the signature of a marking problem, not a demand problem.
Fewer spam messages arrived, which is good news, and conversion fell for an unrelated reason.

Let's rethink that. It is possible, but the two falling together points somewhere more specific: spam that is never marked stays in the real pile, which is exactly what pushes conversion down. Check whether anyone has used Junk? this month before concluding demand changed.
The period selector is on Today for one figure and Month for the other.

Let's rethink that. It is the right instinct — period mismatches cause a lot of confusion here — but both of these are month figures by definition, so one selector governs them together. The denominator is the thing to look at.
The record behind the conversation: status tabs, quick actions, and the booking wizard.
Care Command is the queue; this is the ledger
A conversation can be closed while the person still needs something. The contact is what the Dashboard counts and what the next operator inherits, and these tabs are its lifecycle.
New → Lead → Appointment Scheduled → Service Used
Four forward states and one branch off to the side for Cancelled / Spam. Moving forward happens because something real happened; it is never a tidy-up.
Six people, six different next actions
The same list holds a booked client, a lead, an active enquiry, someone still thinking, someone to re-contact and a spam entry. The status is what tells you what to do next — the row order does not.
Book runs a duplicate check — read it
The wizard offers plausible matches before it creates anything. Confirming the wrong suggested client writes the visit — and later the clinical note — into another person's record.

Scope: a real visit, a real slot on a real nurse's day, and the money that follows it. Reversible: the booking can be cancelled, but a clinical note written against the wrong client is a correction someone has to make by hand. Check first: the phone number, not the name — two people can share a surname and a district.
Spam is not a way to clear the list
Marking spam also flags the phone number, so a real family member starts pre-judged the next time they call. Use it for junk, not for tidiness.
A lost booking without a reason is invisible
Booking Lost with no reason cannot be analysed, so the same cause repeats all quarter. Eighteen were lost this month; a reason on each is what turns that into something you can fix.
You are booking a home visit. The duplicate check offers two clients with the same surname in the same district; one has the phone number the caller just gave you. What do you do?
Match on the phone number, and if anything still looks off, confirm the date of birth before creating the booking.

Yes. The phone number is the identifier the caller just confirmed; the name is the one that collides. Anything still ambiguous is worth thirty seconds of checking, because the alternative is a clinical note in the wrong record.
Pick the first suggestion — the wizard ranks the most likely match at the top.

Let's rethink that. Ranking is a guess about likelihood, not a statement of identity, and it has no access to the number the caller just read out to you. The check exists precisely because the top suggestion is sometimes the wrong person.
Create a new contact to be safe, and merge the records later.

Let's rethink that. A new record splits this person's history in two: their consents, their past visits and their balance stay on the old one. "Merge later" is work that usually never happens, and until it does the next operator sees half a patient.
The team's shared follow-up board — every scheduled call, meeting, email and task.
Nine open promises, grouped by kind

4 to-dos, 3 calls, 1 meeting, 1 email — nine in total. That is exactly the Dashboard's Pending Follow-ups card. If the two ever disagree, an activity was closed without the contact's status being updated.
A promise made on Monday is only kept if it is visible on Thursday
This board is the difference between “we'll call you back” and being called back. Nothing else in CRM remembers a commitment that has no message attached to it.
Overdue items are not inside Today
Filtering to Today shows what is due today — not what was due yesterday and never happened. The overdue work is the work most likely to become a complaint, and it is exactly what that filter hides.
Scope: nothing changes when you filter — but what you cannot see, you will not do. Reversible: yes, immediately. Check first: clear the date filter at least once a shift, and again before handover.
Scheduling on yourself hides the work
An activity assigned to one person is invisible as team work. If that person is off sick, the promise simply does not happen and nobody finds out until the client calls.
Two lines in the note — what was promised, and by when — is what makes an activity handoverable.
Close the activity and update the contact
Closing an activity without recording the outcome turns the board green while the contact's status stays wrong — and then the Dashboard reports something that is not true.
It is 16:50, just before handover at 17:00. The Activities board filtered to Today is empty. What should you do before you leave?
Clear the date filter and check for overdue items, then hand over anything still open by name.

Yes. An empty Today is not an empty board — overdue work sits outside that filter, and it is the work most likely to become tomorrow's complaint. Handing it over by name is what stops it waiting another day.
Nothing — an empty board means the day's follow-ups are done.

Let's rethink that. Today shows what is due today, and it says nothing about what was due yesterday and never happened. The filter is doing exactly what it says; the risk is reading it as "nothing outstanding".
Schedule tomorrow's follow-ups on yourself so nothing is forgotten overnight.
Let's rethink that. Scheduling ahead is good, but putting it all on yourself is what makes it invisible as team work — and you are about to be off shift. Assign it where the next person will see it.
Things that arrived on a channel but carried too little to become a conversation.
Real people who arrived with too little

Three arrivals today: a Facebook comment with no phone number, a half-finished web form, and a Zalo message to an account still in setup. Each is somebody who reached out and would otherwise vanish between systems.
These records are evidence, not drafts
They hold exactly what the channel sent, and nothing else. That immutability is what lets you tell the difference between “the customer gave no number” and “someone deleted it”.
Converting needs at least one anchor

A contact, a phone number or an email address — at least one. The first row has none, so Convert is refused rather than allowed to create an unreachable record. A contact nobody can call is worse than no contact at all.
For that first row the useful action is on Facebook, not here: reply to the comment and ask for a number.
Dismissing is a judgement, and it has your name on it
Dismiss records “this was not a patient”. It is recorded against you, and it is the right action when it is true. What it is not is a way to clear the badge count.

Scope: this arrival only — no contact is created and no message is sent. Reversible: the record stays and can be reviewed, but the person is not contacted in the meantime. Check first: is there really no way to reach them, or is the anchor just on another channel?
Once or twice a shift — and always after a campaign
Campaign traffic is where half-identified arrivals come from. The volume here jumping is usually the first sign that an advert is pointing somewhere that does not capture a phone number.
A Facebook comment arrives: “có nhận chăm sóc tại nhà không ạ?” with no phone number and no linked profile. Convert is greyed out. What is the right move?
Reply on Facebook asking how to reach them, and leave the arrival here until there is an anchor.
Yes. The missing piece is a way to reach the person, and the place to get it is the channel they used. The arrival stays visible so it does not get lost while you wait.
Dismiss it — without a number there is nothing this desk can do.

Let's rethink that. Dismiss records that this was not a patient, and that is not what happened here: this is a real enquiry that simply arrived without a number. Ask for one on the channel it came from — the comment is still open.
Create a contact by hand with the Facebook name so it stops sitting in this queue.

Let's rethink that. That produces a contact nobody can call, which is exactly what Convert refuses to do for you — and it now counts in the Dashboard as a real enquiry that can never convert. The queue is not the problem; the missing number is.
Every arrival from the website, with the advert or link that produced it.
Thirty-four website enquiries this month: 19 from the Hà Nội home-nursing campaign, 11 from the August wound-care advert, and 4 with no UTM captured at all.
34 is the same Website row you will see on Lead Analysis. If they differ, one of the two is filtered to a different period.
Unmatched campaigns is a leak, not a rounding error
Four arrivals carry no campaign. They are real enquiries whose source is unknown, which means the advert that paid for them gets no credit — and the one wasting money keeps running.

Scope: nothing here changes a record — this screen is read-only. Reversible: not applicable. Check first: before you conclude a campaign is failing, check how many of its arrivals landed in Unmatched instead.
A touchpoint joins by phone number, not by channel

Trần Mỹ Linh clicked a Google advert on 10 August and read the wound-care page without filling in the form. Two days later she messaged the Zalo OA — and the touchpoint attached to that conversation by phone number.
This is why a Zalo enquiry can legitimately be credited to a website campaign. The channel it arrived on is not always the thing that produced it.
Read it next to Lead Analysis, never alone

This screen tells you where arrivals came from. It does not tell you whether they became bookings — that is the pivot on Lead Analysis. Volume without outcome is how a busy campaign gets mistaken for a good one.
The wound-care advert shows 11 arrivals and your manager says it is underperforming against the 19 from the home-nursing campaign. What do you check first?
How many of the 4 unmatched arrivals belong to it, and how many of each campaign's arrivals actually became bookings.

Yes. Eleven versus nineteen is a volume comparison, and volume is not the outcome. Unmatched arrivals can belong to either campaign, and a campaign with fewer arrivals that converts better is the one you want more of.
Nothing to check — 11 is fewer than 19, so the advert is underperforming.

Let's rethink that. That compares how many people arrived, not how many became patients. Four arrivals this month carry no campaign at all, so the two counts are not even complete — and neither one says anything about bookings.
Check the Dashboard's Conversion Rate to see whether the adverts are working.

Let's rethink that. Conversion Rate is one number for every channel together — Zalo, hotline, walk-in and all. It cannot separate two website campaigns from each other. The pivot on Lead Analysis is where that comparison lives.
The pivot: enquiries by source, status, service and area — the whole funnel in one grid.
THE WHOLE FUNNEL IN ONE GRID
Channel down the side, outcome across the top
Every enquiry this month appears exactly once, at the intersection of the channel it belongs to and what happened to it. Zalo 96, hotline 58, website 34, Facebook 21, walk-in 9, referral 6.
It must add up to the Dashboard, or one of them is filtered differently

The totals row reads 63 booked, 129 leads, 18 lost, 14 spam, 224 in all — the same four numbers as the Dashboard. When they disagree, the cause is almost always a different period or a different catchment area, not a broken report.

Zalo brings 96 enquiries and books 31. The hotline brings 58 and books 19. Zalo is bigger; the hotline converts at almost the same rate on half the volume. Those are two different pieces of information and only one of them is on the Dashboard.
The interesting column is usually Lost, not Booked: it is where a fixable cause hides.
A cell is a group of people, not a verdict
Every cell opens the records behind it. Before recommending that a channel be cut, open its Lost column and read why those enquiries were lost — the reason is often nothing to do with the channel.

Scope: reading changes nothing here, but a recommendation made from this grid changes where the clinic spends. Reversible: a decision is, the quarter is not. Check first: that the period and catchment match the figures you are comparing against, and that Lost has reasons recorded.
Referral shows 6 enquiries, 1 booked and 2 spam. Someone proposes dropping referrals from the reporting entirely. What is the best response?
Open the six records first — with numbers this small, two spam entries could be one mis-marked caller, and the conclusion changes completely.
Yes. Six is small enough to read individually, and at that size a single mis-marking moves the rate enormously. Decisions about a channel deserve the records, not just the row.
Agree — one booking out of six is a poor return and the volume is negligible.

Let's rethink that. At six enquiries, one record either way swings the rate by a sixth, so the number is too small to carry a decision on its own. Referrals also tend to arrive already trusting the clinic — worth reading before removing.
Compare it with the Dashboard's Conversion Rate to settle the question.

Let's rethink that. The Dashboard's rate is every channel combined, so it cannot say anything about referrals specifically — comparing a single row against it would just be comparing referrals with themselves plus everyone else. This grid is already the per-channel view.
Every visit for the day, and the four things you can do to one.
Fourteen visits, and one of them has nobody

Every visit for Wednesday 12 August in Hà Nội: 13 assigned and 1 unassigned. Each row carries the time, the patient, the service, the district and who is on it — a visit exists here as a whole thing, not as a row on somebody's schedule.
The row order is time, not priority. The one that needs you is not at the top.
Unassigned at 15:00 is a phone call waiting to happen
B-4474, Hoàng Thị Yến, an injection in Cầu Giấy at 15:00, with nobody on it. Unassigned in the morning is a scheduling task. Unassigned in the afternoon is a family ringing to ask where the nurse is.
This is the same booking the Operations Dashboard counts in its Unassigned card. One number, one list, one job.
Assign puts a person on it. Reschedule moves it in time and keeps everything else. Start service moves it to In Progress. Cancel ends it — the visit, the slot and the revenue together.
Cancel is not a stronger reschedule

Cancelling ends the visit. The patient is not rebooked, the slot is not offered to anyone else, and the revenue is gone. If what you actually want is a different time or a different person, those are two other buttons.

Scope: this visit, the slot it occupied, and the money attached to it. Reversible: no — a new booking is a new booking, and the patient has already been told. Check first: whether the family wants a different time rather than no visit, and whether another person could take it.
B-4471 is conversation #4172 from the CRM desk
Nguyễn Thị Hoa, wound care at home, 16:30 in Cầu Giấy. On the CRM desk this is the booking that pushed her conversation to 110 — a visit inside 24 hours adds +30. Same patient, same day, two screens.
Moving this booking changes that urgency score. Operations and the CRM desk are looking at one day from two sides.
Assigned is a plan; In Progress is a fact

Today: 2 completed, 3 in progress, 8 still assigned or new, 1 cancelled. Only the nurse can turn Assigned into In Progress by starting the service — if that never happens, the visit did not happen, whatever the schedule says.
A family rings at 14:00: the patient has gone to hospital and will not be home for the 15:00 visit. What do you do to booking B-4474?
Reschedule it, so the visit and the money survive and the family is not asked to start again.

Yes. Nothing about this says the patient no longer needs the visit — only that today does not work. Reschedule keeps the booking, the client link and the revenue, and frees the slot for someone else today.
Cancel it — the visit is not happening today, and that is what cancel is for.

Let's rethink that. Cancel ends the visit, the slot and the revenue, and the family has to start again from an enquiry. What actually changed is the time, not the need — and there is a button for exactly that.
Leave it and let the nurse find out when she arrives — she may be able to see someone else nearby.
Let's rethink that. A nurse travelling to an empty house costs the visit anyway, plus her time and the next patient's punctuality. You know now; the schedule can still be changed now.
Who is doing what, all day — the screen an Operations Manager lives in.
Ngọc 5, Lan 4, Hà 3, Tuấn 1. Bookings tells you what was promised; this tells you whether it can be done by the people who are actually here today.
Thirteen, not fourteen. The unassigned booking is on nobody's row — which is exactly why it is easy to miss here.
An empty row is not a free nurse
Tuấn has one visit and a lot of white space. That white space is not availability — it is a person in Long Biên with travel time on either side of everything you might add.

Ngọc is at 5 of 6 and Tuấn at 1 of 6. That looks unbalanced and might not be: five visits inside Ba Đình is a lighter day than three spread across the city. Read the bars next to the districts, never alone.
Equal counts across unequal distances is not fairness. It is just a tidier chart.
Long Biên at 15:00, Cầu Giấy at 16:30
A 90-minute gap and a 50-minute journey. It fits — with 40 minutes of slack in Hà Nội afternoon traffic. The schedule would have shown you a comfortable gap and told you nothing about the distance.

Scope: nothing is changed by looking. But a reassignment made without looking becomes a nurse who is late, a family who waited, and a next visit that starts behind. Reversible: the assignment is, the afternoon is not. Check first: the district on both visits, not just the times.
You can save an infeasible leg on purpose

The checker tells you and then lets you proceed. That is deliberate: a manager on the phone to a family often knows something the map does not — that they will wait, or that the building has a lift, or that this nurse lives on that street.
The absence of a warning is not a promise either. It knows distance; it does not know weather, lifts, or how long a family keeps you at the door.

Hà has requested the 13th; Tuấn is approved for the 14th to 16th. Approving a request makes that person unavailable — it does not reassign the visits already booked for those days. Those stay exactly where they are until somebody moves them.

Scope: one person's availability, across the dates approved. Reversible: the approval is, but the days between now and then are not. Check first: open this schedule for every approved date before you approve, not after — that is the only moment the cost is still cheap.
Hà asks for the 13th off. You open the schedule for the 13th and she has three visits booked, two of them in Hai Bà Trưng. What is the right order of actions?
Find who can take the three visits first, then approve the leave once they have somewhere to go.

Yes. Approval does not move a visit, so approving first creates three visits belonging to someone who will not be there — and nothing on any screen will shout about it. Reassign first and the approval costs nothing.
Approve the leave first so the schedule is accurate, then reassign from the gap it creates.

Let's rethink that. It sounds orderly, but approval does not create a gap — it leaves three visits assigned to someone who is on leave, and they look completely normal on the schedule. The accuracy you are hoping for is the thing that does not happen.
Approve it and tell Hà to hand the three visits over herself before she goes.

Let's rethink that. Reassigning someone else's visit needs Operations — it is not available to the nurse whose visit it is, so you would be asking her to do something the system will not let her do. The handover has to happen on this screen.
